newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac tries to placate judges after damning report.
newsitem.headline: Chirac tries to placate judges after damning report.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac sought on Thursday to placate judges who accused him of interfering with the justice system by insisting on the appointment of key law officials.

"The task of guaranteeing the independence of judicial authority belongs to the president, elected by universal suffrage. I attach great importance to this responsibility and...am determined to exercise it to the utmost," Chirac said.

Chirac spoke as the Higher Magistrates' Council (CSM), the independent judiciary watchdog, presented him with its annual report in which it accuses him of insisting on the appointment of key law officials against its advice.

The report supports charges by the opposition Socialists that Chirac was packing the judiciary to stonewall investigations involving alleged illicit funding of his ruling RPR party via kickbacks on public housing contracts while he was mayor of Paris in 1977-95.
But Chirac reminded the CSM that its role was only consultative, and that judicial appointments were the constitutional prerogative of the president.
"I am indeed happy to benefit from the proposals or opinion of figures recognised by the judicial world which enable me to exercise the power of appointment I hold," Chirac said.

In excerpts of the report published by the left-wing daily Liberation on Wednesday, the CSM complains that Chirac overruled it in nearly half the cases in which it had opposed particular appointments.
The CSM complained that its recommendations against certain appointments had been overridden in 46 percent of cases in 1996. "This is a break with past practice," it was quoted as saying.

The report, which recommends that the justice minister be stripped of the power to order sensitive probes pursued or shelved, is an embarrassment for Chirac, who publicly called in January for reforms to uphold the justice system's independence.
The government in July filled the jobs of Paris Appeals Court and Supreme Court prosecutors with Alexandre Benmakhlouf and Jean-Francois Burgelin, former aides to Chirac and Toubon.

Under Benmakhlouf's control are all magistrates probing allegations of kickbacks at the Paris housing authority to feed Gaullist slush funds, the allocation of low-rent city-owned housing to relatives and political cronies and several other scandals involving the RPR and its allies.
In August, the government appointed a magistrate close to the Gaullist party as director of criminal affairs and pardons, a highly sensitive Justice Ministry position.
